newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin caution worries French right, unions.
newsitem.headline: Jospin caution worries French right, unions.

text.p: Opposition politicians and France's powerful trade unions expressed concern on Friday over new leftist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's go-slow approach to key economic decisions though union leaders praised his goals.

Following Jospin's first live television appearance since he took power a month ago, rightist parliamentarians accused him of hypocrisy in blaming fiscal woes on the previous conservative government and in his handling of the controversial closing of a Renault auto assembly plant in Belgium.

Key union leaders urged the Socialist head of government to move more swiftly to implement potentially costly campaign promises to create 700,000 new jobs and trim the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss in pay.

Jospin stressed pragmatism and patience and turned his back on ideology in the interview, reaffirming his commitment to launching a single European currency while tackling public deficits and trying to fight unemployment, boost social justice and preserve fragile economic growth.
He acknowledged the job was a challenging one and blamed his difficulties in part on financial woes inherited from the previous government.
Concerning Renault's plan to close its plant in Vilvoorde, which Jospin had pledged to review during his parliamentary election campaign, the prime minister said he had kept his word.
Though the plant will still close, he boasted that some workers would be redeployed and none would be laid off outright.
Gaullist RPR parliamentarian Patrick Devedjian accused Jospin of raising false hopes in pledging to review Renbault's decision to close the Vilvoorde plant.
"Closing the plant was inevitable, and delaying its closing would only cause Renault to lose market share," he told Radio Monte Carlo.
"What strikes me is that he is wasting time. He has said he wants to take his time but he is wasting it," Devedjian said.

Financial markets were ripe for a resumption of planned privatisations interrupted by the leftists' arrival in power and autumn was too late for a decision on whether to rejig the 1997 budget in order to meet France's commitment to European economic and monetary union, he said.

Former rightist budget minister Alain Lamassoure, interviewed separately on Europe 1 radio, accused Jospin of seeking to avoid responsibility for his policies by blaming budget woes on the previous government.

Lamassoure, a member of the centrist UDF who lost his seat in the June 1 parliamentary election, denounced Jospin's decision to order an audit of public finances, due on July 21, before making key decisions on spending and economic policies.
Jospin well knew the state of public finances when he took office, Lamassoure said.

"The economic situation is better than it has been. Their situation is less difficult that the previous government found when it came to power," said Gaullist former transport Bernard Pons on France 2 television.

Marc Blondel, leader of the giant Socialist-dominated Force Ouvriere (FO) union, urged Jospin to take quick steps, before the autumn, to help create jobs and praised the overall tone of the prime minister's remarks.

"Business leaders and the financial community have already launched an intensive battle to influence his decisions" on the economy and jobs, said the communist-led Confederation Generale du Travail (CGT) in a statement.
